warnings: General information, not medical advice. Check with a doctor before starting calcium supplements.
Food first: the Endocrine Society of India advises meeting calcium needs from food and using supplements only when diet cannot meet needs or needs are higher.

Total calcium from food and supplements above 2,500 mg/day (2,000 mg/day from age 51) is above the US/EFSA upper limits; high supplement doses can cause constipation, high blood calcium (hypercalcaemia), kidney stones and, with antacids, milk-alkali syndrome.
Single supplement doses above about 500 mg are absorbed less well; split larger amounts.
Calcium can block absorption of levothyroxine, iron, some antibiotics (tetracyclines, quinolones) and bisphosphonates; gaps of several hours are advised, so ask a pharmacist or doctor.
Thiazide-type water pills reduce calcium loss in urine, so calcium and vitamin D supplements need medical supervision.
In chronic kidney disease, total calcium intake (food plus calcium-based binders) is set by the kidney team; never self-supplement.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding calcium supplements are prescribed by the doctor or health programme; the app never sets the dose.

conditionAdjustments.change: Food target stays at the adult value; India's national programme (2014) provides 500 mg elemental calcium with vitamin D3 250 IU daily and WHO advises 1500-2000 mg/day only where dietary intake is low; the 2024 NEJM India/Tanzania trials found 500 mg/day not clearly worse than 1500 mg/day for pre-eclampsia. Dose is set by the doctor; requires doctor input
